article_title: Mullin confirmed as homeland security secretary
article_content:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Confirmation by the U.S. Senate on March 23 elevated Cherokee Nation citizen and Oklahoma Republican Markwayne Mullin to one of the most potent law enforcement posts in the federal government – secretary of the Department of Homeland Security.
Cherokee Nation Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Jr. said the confirmation is significant to the CN and Indian Country overall.
“As a Cherokee Nation citizen, his service on the national stage carries deep meaning,” Hoskin said “We will miss his leadership in the Senate but know he will serve the country well in such a critical role on the world and national stage.”
Hoskin mentioned the challenges Mullin faces.
“This is a critical time for DHS,” Hoskin said. “As DHS secretary, Senator Mullin can focus the agency better on law and order, fiscal discipline, public safety, emergency response, federal and tribal relations, and most critically a commitment to due process and respect for the dignity of all human life. We wish him success in this new role as he works to protect the nation while carrying forward the values that have long guided our families and communities.”
Mullin grew up in Westville – roughly 30 miles east of the CN capital in Tahlequah. He is an enrolled CN member, the first tribal citizen to serve in the Senate in nearly two decades and the second CN citizen ever to serve in the chamber.
Mullin spoke to many of his colleagues at his confirmation hearing the previous week before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
“I’m not scared of a challenge,” he said. “I am scared of failure, and so I will work hard each day. My goal in six months is that we’re not in the lead story every single day.”
But Mullin now leads an organization in tumult. DHS funding lapsed on Feb. 14, and though lawmakers and the Trump administration continue negotiations to end the shutdown, a deal remains out of reach. The confirmation vote came amid wide public aversion to the immigration crackdown and deportations under DHS, and the ongoing partial shutdown of the department.
Mullin arrives when public support for the president’s immigration agenda has fallen after a year of high-profile operations in multiple American cities. Under former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem’s leadership, officers were accused of using imprudent force and even illegal methods to arrest immigrants, detaining them in squalid conditions and bypassing due process. Two protesters – both U.S. citizens – were shot to death in Minneapolis by immigration agents under DHS control.
The DHS shutdown has become of particular concern to tribal communities. ICE agents arrested several Native Americans during the federal immigration crackdown in Minneapolis, precipitating tension and confusion as communication was deficient between agencies and tribes over their whereabouts. The Oglala Sioux tribe cited sovereignty to ban ICE from entering the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota.
During his confirmation hearing, Mullin signaled a possible different approach than Noem on immigration enforcement.
“I would love to see ICE become more a transport than on the front line,” Mullin told senators, and pledged to require ICE officers to obtain judicial warrants before entering private property, with limited exceptions.
A pair of Democrats – Sens. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico – voted with most Senate Republicans in favor of Mullin’s appointment. Heinrich, who served with Mullin in the House, explained his endorsement.
“I have also seen first-hand that Markwayne is not someone who can simply be bullied into changing his views, and I look forward to having a secretary who doesn’t take their orders from (Deputy White House Chief of Staff) Stephen Miller,” Heinrich said.
Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul was the sole Republican who voted against Mullin’s confirmation. Paul clashed heatedly with Mullin during the hearing, accusing him of having “anger issues” and questioning his fitness to lead federal law enforcement.
“Markwayne Mullin is ready to lead,” said Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming, the No. 2 ranking Republican. He said Mullin will “serve with seriousness and character. He will be a leader who makes our country safer.”
Mullin has supported legislation for advanced appropriations for the Indian Health Service, Bureau of Indian Affairs and Bureau of Indian Education, saying in a 2023 press release: “If the federal government lapses in annual appropriation funding, Indian Country should not have to suffer the consequences.”
Osage Nation Principal Chief Geoffrey Standing Bear offered his support ahead of the confirmation.
“Senator Mullin understands the unique co-governing relationship tribal nations share with state and federal governments, and he is a strong voice for collaboration that benefits everyone who resides within our territory,” Standing Bear said.
Mullin has been candid about his CN citizenship in Washington.
“I’m Cherokee, and I never knew I was special for being Cherokee until I came to D.C., because where I’m from, everybody’s Indian or wants to be," Mullin once said during a Senate Indian Affairs Committee hearing.
The White House said on March 23 that it had been waiting until Mullin was confirmed before continuing to negotiate with Democrats over the DHS shutdown.
Mullin was sworn in on March 24.
